title: Cultural Dissemination: An Agent-Based Model with Social Influence
publisher: Journal of Artificial Societies and Social Simulation (JASSS) 24(4) 5; Nguyen, Chen, Jin, Quinn, Tyler, Landsberg

key_points.claim: Axelrod model basics: homophily + assimilation on a grid; can yield persistent diversity (absorbing states with distinct cultural regions) rather than a single monoculture.
key_points.evidence_quote: the model predicts in some cases the persistence of diversity

key_points.claim: Adding neighborhood social influence (many-to-one) via a probabilistic switching rule Q = O(j trait)/(O(i trait)+O(j trait)) amplifies cultural heterogeneity vs Axelrod.
key_points.evidence_quote: the more one allows individual agents to be influenced by other agents in their local environment, the less homogeneous the resulting society becomes

key_points.claim: Quantitative comparison on 30x30 grid, F=5, Q=10: social influence gives ~8.0 frozen zones vs 1.34 for Axelrod; more events (23.5M vs 7.4M) but fewer interactions (376k vs 1.82M).

Lattice size effect: in Axelrod, frozen zones rise then fall past ~6x6 (monoculture prevails); in the social influence model they keep increasing with size, explained by competition between multiplicity effect and dominant-regions effect, with social influence making zones robust.
key_points.evidence_quote: in the Social Influence Model the number of zones steadily increases

key_points.claim: Mechanism: social influence hardens local consensus so zones resist infiltration by distant regions; final monoculture differed from initial dominant region in ~63% of Axelrod trials vs ~9% for social influence.
key_points.evidence_quote: social influence produces a hardening of opinions within local zones that are relatively robust to external influences

key_points.claim: Three new heterogeneity metrics: neighbor dissimilarity, configurational entropy of region sizes, and geometric roughness/elongation of regions; applicable to other cultural dissemination models.
key_points.evidence_quote: The quantitative metrics introduced in this paper have broad potential applicability across a large variety of agent-based cultural dissemination models.

key_points.claim: Boundary conditions and neighborhood size matter: periodic boundaries reduce frozen zones in both models; a larger neighborhood (12 vs 4) lowers zone count (8.0 to 6.7) and raises moderate-size zones.
key_points.evidence_quote: boundary effects can still play an important role even in large systems

key_points.claim: Axelrod model has a first-order order-disorder transition for F>2; the social influence model at F=5 shows no corresponding discontinuous transition. A stripped-down Flache & Macy (2011) model shows similar heterogeneity growth, suggesting robust mechanism.
key_points.evidence_quote: for the Social Influence Model at \(F=5\) there does *not* exist a corresponding discontinous (first-order) transition

key_points.claim: Literature context: extensions of Axelrod include mass media, cultural drift/noise, complex networks, neighborhood size, and opinion dynamics/bounded confidence models (Deffuant, Hegselmann-Krause).
key_points.evidence_quote: the effect of a “mass media” agent was studied by Shibanai et al. (2001)

reliability_notes: Full text peer-reviewed JASSS article with open code (Python, CoMSES). Simulation-based on abstract lattice models; findings limited to tested parameter ranges (authors caution asymptotic trend may not hold for larger lattices). Focused on culture/opinion dynamics only.
